assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade, productivity and welfare are modeled. It supplies the standard framework for the extensive margin, reallocation and gains from trade, and it connects to growth and firm-dynamics work. Its reach across theory, quantification and empirics is very large.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman's work on trade with monopolistic competition and on firm-level exporting and FDI decisions (with Melitz and Yeaple) completes the core. Redding is important for quantitative extensions but seems more derivative. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on this ballot, contributed closely related early work.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets and countries. It is now textbook material, so timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Credit sharing with Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum, who are outside this entry.
Whether the committee sees this as a sufficiently distinct step after the earlier new-trade-theory prize.
Helpman also has other candidacies on the list (B044), so the right grouping is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework is the workhorse of monetary policy analysis in central banks. It combines nominal rigidities, microfoundations and policy rules. Its practical and scientific influence is very high.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people. Woodford gave the systematic microfounded policy framework, Gali (with Gertler and Clarida) the empirical and analytical canon, and Taylor staggered contracts and the Taylor rule. Calvo supplied the pricing device. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans developed the medium-scale DSGE model and the identification of monetary shocks. Smets and Wouters are also credited here. A three-name cap forces hard choices, and Clarida, Rotemberg and Mankiw are not on the ballot.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The framework has been used for roughly 25 years and was tested in the 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound episode and the post-pandemic inflation.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution and the three-name limit.
Debate over the framework's performance in the post-2021 inflation and its handling of heterogeneity.
Whether Gertler or Christiano-Eichenbaum should be preferred to the names proposed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance made legal institutions and investor protection a core empirical explanation of financial development and corporate governance. It is highly cited and shaped the institutions literature that two recent prizes touched. The broader Shleifer-Vishny agenda (corporate governance, limits to arbitrage) strengthens the case.
assessment.attribution: The four-author core (LLSV) is clear. I propose the three who led the legal-origins and anti-self-dealing work, and Vishny is the omitted fourth. Shleifer's wider work in behavioral finance and corporate governance adds further claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 25+ years of influence. Replications and critiques have refined the findings.
uncertainties: Legal-origins empirical claims have been challenged on measurement and causal grounds.
Possible overlap in the committee's mind with the 2024 institutions prize.
Whether the committee would limit credit to Shleifer alone, or include Vishny.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income and wealth series built from tax data reshaped the measurement of inequality and public debate, and they underlie major modern work in public economics. The measurement contribution is real and is complemented by Saez's optimal-tax work (B014).
assessment.attribution: Piketty-Saez (2003) is the foundation, and Zucman is a prominent younger contributor on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts. Atkinson, who is deceased, was an early pioneer of top-income series. The theoretical claims in Capital in the Twenty-First Century are more contested than the data work.
assessment.maturity: The data work is mature (20+ years). The interpretation and policy implications are still contested.
uncertainties: Contested theory and policy claims, and the risk of the prize being read as politically charged.
Whether Zucman's contribution is mature enough for inclusion.
Measurement critiques of the distributional series.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson and Tabellini built a systematic, formal-plus-empirical political economics of electoral rules, constitutions and fiscal outcomes. The agenda is influential and has a substantial literature. Besley adds work on state capacity.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clear core (the Political Economics book and the constitutions papers). Besley's state-capacity work with Persson is a closely related strand. It is a coherent trio.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 30 years of development and many empirical follow-ups.
uncertainties: Possible fatigue with political-economy and institutions topics after the 2024 prize.
Persson's links to the committee and IIES (a conflict to be disclosed, not adjudicated).
Credibility of some cross-country empirical identification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Social preferences (reciprocity, fairness, inequity aversion) provided a disciplined alternative to pure self-interest. They have been tested experimentally and applied to contracts and cooperation. The influence on behavioral economics and neighbouring fields is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Fehr-Schmidt (1999) is the canonical model. Fehr's experimental program (with Gächter and others) is central. Falk's contributions are strong but later. Rabin (B046) and Bolton-Ockenfels, who are not listed here, overlap in credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, 25+ years, with many replications. There is also a controversy about external validity.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with Rabin and Bolton-Ockenfels.
Behavioral economics has already been recognized (Kahneman, Thaler).
Lab-to-field generalization.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed how economists understand labor-demand shifts, polarization and local adjustment. The agenda is highly influential in research and policy and connects trade, labor and technology, including AI.
assessment.attribution: The task approach draws on Autor-Levy-Murnane and Acemoglu-Autor, and the China shock on Autor-Dorn-Hanson. Katz has a long record on skill premia (with Goldin and Murphy). The proposed three are the trade-shock core, while Acemoglu (already a laureate) is a key task-theory contributor.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature (about 10-20 years). Some conclusions about durability of local effects are still being tested.
uncertainties: Lasting effects and identification debates around the China shock.
Credit overlap with Acemoglu-Restrepo and Katz.
Whether the committee would favor Autor alone, or a task-based group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation across firms offered a quantitative explanation of cross-country income and TFP differences. It gave a measurable mechanism linking micro frictions to aggregate productivity and shaped growth, development and macro-trade work. Evidence at scale, with large policy relevance for development.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) and Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) are the twin foundations. Restuccia-Rogerson is a counterpart paper whose first author, Richard Rogerson, is not credited here. The three proposed names are reasonable but not exhaustive. Banerjee-Duflo and Jovanovic have related work. I disclose that I collaborate with Klenow, which makes my ranking of this entry cautious, and I place it last for that reason.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature (about 15 years), with many follow-ups and critiques about measurement of distortions.
uncertainties: Personal conflict: long-running co-authorship with Klenow.
Whether measured wedges truly reflect misallocation or measurement error and heterogeneity in fundamentals.
The Rogerson omission and attribution among growth-accounting contributors.
